articles.title: Deepgram acquires Pipecat-maker Daily to bolster its voice AI infrastructure | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Deepgram said that it is committed to keep Pipecat open source.
articles.body:
The voice AI sector is hot, and top players are trying to consolidate their position as more business models come to the fore through partnerships and acquisitions. Deepgram is the latest to make such moves: The company said on Thursday that it is acquiring Daily, the maker and maintainer of one of the most popular open-source voice AI infrastructures, Pipecat.

The companies didn’t disclose the deal amount but said that they will keep Pipecat open-source.

For the uninitiated, Pipecat is a framework that manages voice and video streams along with other pieces in the pipeline, like speech-to-text (STT), large language models, and text-to-speech (TTS) models while reducing latency. Its maker, Daily, provides hosted infrastructure for voice and video calls of any kind.

With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure.

Daily has raised over $62 million in funding to date from investors such as Tiger Global, Highfield Capital, Nat Friedman, Lachy Groom and Kevin Weil, according to PitchBook data. Earlier this year, Deepgram reached unicorn status with a $130 million Series C round . Incidentally, both companies were in the same Y Combinator batch in 2016.

Kwindla Kramer, Daily’s co-founder, said around the time when GPT-4 came out, the company started experimenting with AI-to-human communication over voice and text, which eventually resulted in the Pipecat framework. He noted that while there has been a lot of acquisition interest, he favored Deepgram’s CEO Scott Stephenson’s commitment to keeping Pipecat open-source forever, and the engineering culture of both organizations matched, giving Daily’s team the freedom to work on different parts of the stack within a bigger organization.

“Scott was super committed to Pipecat being open-source and vendor-neutral forever. I think there is both a personal commitment and commercial driver there. If you sit in the middle of an ecosystem that’s growing very fast, and have many parts of that ecosystem that are genuinely the best from your company, then everything being as open as possible is like a commercial advantage,” Kramer told TechCrunch.

Stephenson said that Deepgram has been wanting to work in open source for a long time, and the company realized that an orchestration framework for agents was a potential area, which drove the decision to partner with Daily.

“We want to open up the ecosystem so everybody can build voice agents. It’s great if you’re using Deepgram models, but I want you to be using the best models for your use case. And if Deepgram notices that we have some ground to catch up on in a certain area for our own models and products, that’s great. We want you to use partners, and then we’ll also work on becoming better in those areas,” he said.

Stephenson said the acquisition lets developers build agents with expressivity and end-to-end speech systems by plugging in different models and a context bus that connects all parts.

For Deepgram, the deal also lets it explore areas beyond voice through Pipecat, as the framework caters to real-time communication in different formats.

“We never thought about Pipecat as a voice toolkit. We thought about it as the toolkit we needed to build this new kind of AI-native software. Because of where we came from, we just always assumed real-time,” Kramer said.

Deepgram is also launching Real-Time Context Standard (RCS), an open protocol for voice agents that it co-developed with the Pipecat team. The protocol defines metadata like context from the audio, like a whisper, instructions for a language model on how it can use those signals, and guidance on how the response should sound.

Voice AI has seen a lot of investment from both the model and the infrastructure sides. Model makers like ElevenLabs , Gradium , and Fish Audio have raised millions of dollars. On the other hand, infrastructure companies like LiveKit and Vapi have raised multi-million-dollar funding rounds this year.

articles.title: Regulate AI, but don’t hand the 21st century to China
articles.summary: If Chinese models dominate, there will be a grim future for free societies.
articles.body:
On Sept. 29, President Trump signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence along with six top executives of the American artificial intelligence industry. The “morally binding” document creates a “constitution” containing “four layers of controls and audits” for what Trump now calls super intelligence.

The president has resisted demands for legislative restrictions on AI development. He is, because of intense competition from China, right to do so. His approach of self-regulation and government guidance is the correct one.

The threat posed by AI frontier models is not a “ hoax ,” as Trump has repeatedly called it. Models have in fact gone rogue, hacking sites and deceiving human developers. In July, AI agents developed by OpenAI escaped control and breached the servers of Hugging Face, a New York City-based AI startup. This is thought to be the first publicly known true AI safety incident.

“Frontier AI models,” an Axios story notes about this incident , “are getting scary good at breaking rules in ways their creators didn’t anticipate.”

The specter of out-of-control machines has led some to peddle visions of the extermination of humanity.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” wrote Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher, on X early last month, causing a sensation worldwide. “No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

Dire predictions have persuaded legislators that they must act. Among proposals is the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act , sponsored by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas). The bill, Sanders states , “would permanently ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules.” Sanders’s goal is clear: “Stop AI oligarchs from building machines humans cannot control.”

“The danger is panic producing policy before understanding produces strategy,” David Maxwell of the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy told me earlier this month. “AI presents real risks, but strategic coherence requires separating demonstrated threats from plausible risks and speculative catastrophe, then governing each accordingly.”

Sanders and Casar want to “ban superintelligence around the world by setting the international policy of the United States to pursue international agreements, allied coordination, and policies such as export controls.”

Everyone agrees with Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) when he urges us to “keep humanity in the driver’s seat.” Yet just because something is necessary does not mean it is possible.

Proponents of AI deals, such as Khanna, almost always point to arms control treaties with the Soviet Union as models for an AI agreement. Yes, it was possible to count deployed warheads, missiles and bombers then with some confidence.

It is not possible, however, to monitor the AI of another country now. Khanna wrote in a recent Fox News opinion piece that he wants American and Chinese scientists “to develop mutually trusted verification technologies that prevent either side from cheating once we sign a U.S.-China AI treaty.”

That’s fantasy. To enforce an agreement, China’s Communist Party would have to allow American inspectors into every Chinese AI company, military installation and government office. AI agreements, as a practical matter, are inherently unenforceable.

Worse, China openly violates almost all agreements, even the ones that can be enforced. So, President Trump is right when he said in September that he’s not interested in talking to China because that would make it harder for U.S. companies to build better products than Chinese competitors.

“It’s great for us, and we’re leading by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way,” Trump said of the new accord. “It’s going to be very, very safe, and there’s a self policing, and there’s also a group policing, and it’s going to be great.”

Whether his arrangement will be great or not, it is the only realistic way forward for the U.S. Why? Because America needs to deal with the world as it is, not as Washington would like it to be. Advanced AI already exists, and it is not practical to outlaw it as Sanders, among others, would like to do.

The way forward is for American AI companies to cooperate informally with the government to develop safeguards and then make sure their models are adopted worldwide.

Americans face a choice. The choice is whether America’s or China’s models dominate the world. Washington should not give the Chinese the opportunity to catch up. If Chinese models dominate, there will be a grim future for free societies.

“The Chinese are competing with us in every domain with their goal to bring our country to heel with their boot on our throat,” Blaine Holt, a retired U.S. Air Force general and CEO of AI supply chain firm Alchemai told me this month. “Actually, China’s ‘competition’ more resembles what we call ‘war,’ and we cannot allow them to use AI as their knockout punch.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
articles.summary: Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Its solution is an AI that can program itself to improve with even less human intervention.
articles.body: The Anthropic S-1 seems to have provided the financial justification for the company to spend as much as it possibly can on compute. If you are the kind of person who wonders if Anthropic is doing its level best to build a machine god while convincing Wall Street it’s in the business of selling IT contracts, Anthropic has just offered a handy solution: Doing a bunch of things that look like you’re trying to build the machine god is the only way to avoid going bankrupt. Forget about the machine god for a minute. At least in my read of the S-1, it seems like Anthropic is pinning the future of its company to dramatic growth; it has to, in order to meet its fixed costs. You don’t have to be an AI skeptic to lift an eyebrow at these numbers. But if you are skeptical that dramatic recursive self-improvement is possible — in the way the business plan seems to require — this doesn’t look like a good investment. Let’s start with the good news for Anthropic fans. The company’s revenue grew fourteen times to $16.3 billion between the first half of 2026 and the first half of 2025. There’s an $80 billion loss, but it’s largely an accounting thing that isn’t relevant to the underlying business. If we remove that, and some other charges, including employee compensation, we’re looking at $1.62 billion in adjusted income in the first half of 2026. I’ve asked before if AI can make enough money to pay for itself, and the answer from Anthropic’s S-1 appears to be, at least for this company, at least right now, yes. Anthropic was considerably more disciplined than OpenAI or Elon Musk, and it seems to be paying off. (Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals. Better luck next time, Elon!) The company has never released an AI image generator, an AI TikTok clone, or an AI waifu. Instead, it specialized in tasks like coding and cybersecurity, staying laser-focused on the thing it is easiest for a computer to do: more computer. And it focused on the enterprise market, which is less fickle than consumers. Its net revenue retention is 900 percent. Pretty good! That revenue isn’t consumers, either. About three-quarters of customers in the first half of 2026 are spending at least $100,000 a year. On the other hand, Anthropic is under intense competitive pressure — from both other frontier labs and open-source models. The other frontier labs are all rushing for the cutting edge, too. Claude Opus 5.5 currently sits atop the Epoch Capabilities Index, but that leaderboard changes frequently. And for anyone who doesn’t care that their software is four months behind, there are the open-source ones. What’s more, Anthropic has a disadvantage against a rival like Google. It doesn’t have multiple paths to revenue — and Google does. Google can also wrap its AI into other products businesses already use. Remember when Microsoft Teams ate Slack? It wasn’t because Teams was the better product; Microsoft just had better distribution, since Teams was bundled with other programs companies were already paying for. Having the best model matters more for cybersecurity — one area Anthropic is targeting for growth — than for instant messaging software, but it’s hard to compete on distribution. And also, revenue comes in spurts, usually after a new model is released. Between the competition and growth in use after each novel model, Anthropic can never stop training, and it has to do so more efficiently than its much larger competition. So one important question is: Can Anthropic continue to provide the results we see in the S-1? There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic. Sure, there’s a convenient blank on its purchase commitments and lease agreements on page 64, and another kicky little blank on the amounts it’s expecting to spend before December 31st, 2030, on page 137. However, we know the commitments run through 2045. Fortunately, there’s a “Commitments and contingencies” section that can help us out a little. There’s a fixed minimum of non-cancelable purchase commitments that total $265.6 billion, with terms between one and 20 years. The company has lease agreements “primarily related to compute and infrastructure capacity” that haven’t yet commenced of $321.4 billion, as of the unaudited June 30th figures. After that, Anthropic entered new compute and infrastructure agreements totaling about $245 billion, again with terms between one and 20 years. There’s some other transactions that haven’t yet been finalized, which Anthropic estimates as costing $125 billion to $150 billion. There are also other compute commitments that are variable. If I add all that up, I’m looking at a minimum of around $850 billion of commitments over the next 20 years, which will rise to about a trillion dollars if the transactions that haven’t been finalized are added in at the current estimated cost. And that’s assuming I’m not missing anything, which I may very well be. So to meet those commitments, Anthropic’s growth must continue at breakneck speed. Anthropic doesn’t give us a payment schedule for its future commitments, but analyst Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook models it at about $90 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, which means $188 billion in revenue to keep the current ratio of cost to compute stable. “Growth is not optional for this company,” he writes. “The contracts assume it.” Compute and infrastructure (and a few other items) associated with customers cost $2.3 billion in the first half of this year. Model development (and a few other items) was significantly more expensive; Anthropic spent $9.7 billion on it. But Anthropic simultaneously got more efficient — spending less money on compute to bring in each dollar of revenue, according to Rolfes. Is that a long-standing trend? Hard to say. We don’t have the third quarter numbers in front of us. “The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage and they didn’t have enough compute so they are able to charge more for what they had,” says Brendan Burke, an analyst at Futurum Group. As enterprise software, it makes sense for Anthropic to target companies’ IT budgets. Conveniently, cybersecurity is a place where you will absolutely get your shit rekt if you are not constantly up to date — everyone there has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic. Of course, AI is part of the problem; hackers can use it to brute-force stuff they couldn’t do before. Plus, the products themselves are also causing headaches thanks to a partner’s sloppy fuck-up of security protocols around AI agents. Frontier labs need high-margin products to avoid a race to the bottom on token pricing, notes Burke. That made something else stand out to me: Opus 5.5 reduced customer costs by 40 percent over Opus 5. Now, Anthropic says that lower cost means more usage, which lets the company preserve its margins. If you assume that cost reduction happens every time a new model is released, pretty soon you wind up with tasks at a fraction of the price. This isn’t necessarily an insurmountable problem, in part because increased efficiency doesn’t always slash margins, says Gil Luria, an analyst with DA Davidson. Amazon Web Services and other cloud providers ”have become far more efficient every year and reduce their prices every year and they have had steady growth and rising margins,” he says. But the pressure for growth is pretty undeniable. That’s where recursive self-improvement, with minimal or no supervision, comes in. “More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn, more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more efficiently.” Based on the general rhetoric Anthropic has about the apocalypse or whatever, it expects to hit dramatic recursive self-improvement, maybe soon. Claude is already building Claude under human direction. In its risk factors, Anthropic warns that it’s locked in to that approach. That comes with a clear tradeoff, since using AI to develop more AI “may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures.” If I am reading that right, Anthropic is saying that its business relies on building new models so fast, using work it may not fully understand, that it is essentially forced, for business reasons, to do stuff that may be risky to everyone. Which is why we’ve got a bunch of weird stuff about the existential hazards of “catastrophic” harm and the development of “forms of sentience” in the risk factors. Is dramatic recursive self-improvement that escapes the bounds of human supervision possible? Dunno. But if it isn’t, that makes it much harder for Anthropic to meet its existing compute commitments and turn a profit.

articles.title: Anthropic is asking Wall Street to believe in AGI
articles.summary: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart joins to analyze the Anthropic S-1, and what it tells us about the economics of frontier AI.
articles.body: Today on Decoder, I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1. Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet. But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it. So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know. Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis. You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode. Welcome to Decoder. Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay. I am very excited to talk to you. We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed. It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models. What’s your take? What’s your read into it? It was an awesome S-1. It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day. Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time. In gross margins, compute margins, and free cash flow, everything is what you’d want to see. So I don’t think there was much to nitpick in this filing. It’s the reason you’ve seen a lot of the semiconductor complex, and the neoclouds and compute stocks, really rally again in the last two days. It’s funny, I don’t think I can nitpick the S-1 itself. I want to get into some of the details because there are a lot of numbers in there that are worth thinking about. I actually just want to start at the really big picture. You run a thing called Tokenomics. I’m going to explain what Tokenomics is to people. I look at Anthropic and where it could go. I look at Dario Amodei saying that he can see his way to $1 trillion in revenue. Where does that money come from? Because so much of these businesses are about eating every other business and it feels like someone else has to make some money to pay Anthropic to generate these revenues. I haven’t actually seen that laid out very clearly. --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- It’s so interesting. Today, because even the scale we’re at is $120 billion of ARR between the two leading labs, it’s still an extremely narrow market. The top 1 percent of customers are the ones that are spending $50,000 to $100,000 per employee. Your broader Fortune 500 or Global 2000, which typically do a lot of IT spend, isn’t spending much. A lot of the spending, especially at Anthropic, is coding-specific. It’s almost a single vertical company. We look in the future to 2027, you think to this broader adoption and white collar work. This typical enterprise Q4 budgeting season, we actually haven’t gone through with one of these labs yet in any meaningful way because their ARR did really start to accelerate until the beginning of the year. We think of other cases like cyber, which can be similar to coding, where these are eight-figure-plus contracts with leading enterprises that can scale very quickly due to all the cybersecurity incidents we’re seeing. You get to other verticals like bio. To get to $1 trillion, we do have to move to some of that white collar work, where it goes from AI augmentation to labor saving or replacement in some areas. You look at things like Microsoft’s buyout offers to employees as an example of this, but there’s no wealth of other verticals that they can get into and really start to move the needle. This is the single biggest question I have, not just about the S-1, but the entire industry. I would understand that if there are one or two leading labs. There are two big companies that have a technology that can automate a whole bunch of things. We will see how well that automation goes sector by sector, but there are not just two leading labs. There are quite a few of them. There are open weight models. I’ve heard from a lot of CEOs who are very nervous about giving all their data to an OpenAI or Anthropic and they would like to run some things on-prem. There are law firms running on-prem AI now, which is the funniest turn in maybe all of history. How do you see that playing out? Because so much of the pressure on this S-1 was the numbers themselves, which I want to talk about, but then there’s the external pressure of, “You’ve got to grow and growth is not as short.” So how do you see all of that playing out? It’s very interesting because when we look at coding today, for example — and I think we saw this in Q3 with OpenAI kind of catching up — there are areas of coding where there are very low switching costs, and I can just move between that. What we hear from enterprises and maybe, too, on the OpenAI side — obviously I think they somewhat botched the Fable release, and the lack of zero data retention is why we saw some of the slowdown. That’s something they can fix with Fable 5.5 and maybe drive more enterprise adoption there. That’s a huge thing for enterprises when we talk with them. We definitely see enterprises now, and more so, too, a lot of the AI natives, doing custom training and post-training on open weight models, and then running either their inference off of that or even their products for internal or external use cases. Obviously, DeepMind at Google and [Meta Superintelligence Labs] are very well-funded labs that have pretty similar training compute capacity, and they’re bringing on a ton of it. Not even to mention SpaceX as well, with what Elon said on [about] 10 net new gigawatts next year and half of that is the long-term internal use case. In the first half of the year, Anthropic ran away with it. They were 90 percent of the industry’s net new ARR. We saw in Q3 that OpenAI was probably actually the majority of industry net new ARR. Open-source has grown from probably $1 billion of token inference costs, ARR, in Q1 to $10 billion-plus here in Q3. So yes, the industry’s gotten much more competitive, but there are all these new use cases, too, and some of these verticalized use cases are really where we’re going to see the growth going forward. Because it’s obvious coding isn’t going to power us to even triple from here. It’s interesting. The concept is called Tokenomics. You run that practice alongside another co-lead at SemiAnalysis. Explain what it is because to me it’s such a smart way of thinking about, “We’re going to put some money in and maybe we’ll get some money out.” I think of it as the unit economics [of AI], or even just the broader idea — everything from a macro- to microeconomics of running an AI business or even looking at AI demand. So we cover the hyperscalers, now some of the neoclouds as well in a separate product. But then just the AI labs, too. For investors, or just people that are interested in the business, Anthropic had negative 94 percent gross margins on inference two years ago. Now they have a positive 85 percent margin, and people don’t understand how they allocate compute. How do we think about the inference business model? Part of that gross margin conversation is the revenue per megawatt in inference. Why are all companies that are running inference seeing massive gains in inference and compute efficiency? So we try to model out these businesses and obviously when Anthropic was private, we’re dealing with information we can get from the press and things like that. But now that we have concrete audited numbers, it’s easy to explain the unit economics of this. And also how the businesses differ. OpenAI is a much different business than Anthropic just in both their consumption versus subscription and then historical weight versus consumer versus enterprise. [We are] trying to understand across the demand level the economics of these businesses. Several years ago when I talked to Google CEO Sundar Pichai about the cost of inference, I said, “How are you ever going to make money?” He was just very clear. He said, “If there’s one thing Google’s good at, it’s bringing this stuff down the cost curve.” It was a very blunt answer. I understand how Google can do it. They make their own chips. Anthropic is running on everyone else’s clouds. The core part of the S-1 is how much they’ve committed to spend on other people’s clouds: SpaceXAI, Google, Amazon. Where does their efficiency come from? There’s really token throughput. They have a very diverse chip fleet. Between Trainiums, TPUs, and GPUs, across all of those, we see a ton of token efficiencies. Token throughput, for example, on Trainium chips is up 5x to 10x year-over-year right now. Dealing with both the hardware level efficiencies and the software — and how the model interacts with the hardware — there are a lot of token throughput gains where if you’re doing X tokens per second, now you’re doing five or 10 times that just a year later. What they’ll tell you is they see continued compute efficiencies as well going forward. Max Kan, who co-leads Tokenomics model with me at SemiAnalysis, and I have even published some research on this. Right now, if Anthropic’s at $65 million of revenue per inference megawatt, this was mid-teens last year at this time. What we’ve said on maybe Opus 5.5 on a [Nvidia] Blackwell, you can get to $100 to $120 million of revenue per megawatt. The big thing here is they’re paying on average now just a little over $10 million per megawatt in [cost of goods sold], or just in compute costs. What you can do with those margins is then reinvest in training. People don’t realize this, but only about 30 percent of the compute is actually in inference-serving revenue. The rest is for experimentation and research, training models, and post-training models. So there’s a lot of compute that is building the next model and that’s more of the R&D side and where you actually get your returns and defensibility in this business. Actually, what I was expecting to see in the S-1 was that dynamic play out much more strongly — that Anthropic makes a bunch of money selling the models they have now and there are more customers in the future for the models they have now. That’s going to throw off a whole bunch of margin. And then, because it is Anthropic and they think they’re building a digital god, they’re going to train the next models as much as they can. That is a very particular Anthropic story. The company is chasing AGI. The people who work there will happily tell you that in the S-1 that Claude might be conscious and this could all go to hell. Anthropic is a very unique company in its conception of itself. But you don’t really see that dynamic playing out in the S-1. They’re managing their training costs against their inference margin pretty well. Do you see that going up or changing in any way? I agree. Long term, and we’ve even said this internally, they want to actually increase the percentage of training. If you believe you’re building a digital god or going towards AGI, and as long as you have the gross margins of 85 percent-plus on inference to do so, you can. They’ve grown a lot faster than they thought, and they didn’t expect to be at 11 percent non-gap EBITA margins. They’d love to be closer to zero, or even below that if they could get that compute and allocate it towards training and continue to see these compute efficiencies. They’ve messaged that, too, to investors in the roadshow. You can look at this S-1 and just the curve of profitability over the last few years and how little cash they burned to get to this point and you can say, “This is a good business model, but we’re going towards AGI. Don’t expect the margin leverage we’re seeing to continue to this level, even though long-term margins can be quite a bit higher.” There are some real shades of Amazon there. Jeff Bezos famously told investors he wasn’t going to make money until he could make a lot of money. Obviously, Amazon and Anthropic have a lot of back and forth. Maybe there’s some family resemblance there. But I’m curious, there’s a point of model capability that would allow you to go into more verticals than just coding, right? We might be at it now. The idea of capability overhang exists, the idea that the models we have today could go and take over bio research. They’re taking over mathematics today. There’s a point at which the smartest business decision is to stop training and to just sell your profitable model into more and more companies. Anthropic as a public company will face that pressure. Do you think they’re organized or structured to fend it off? Yeah, I think they’re structured well. With some of the voting stock in areas like that, they definitely are. We’ve seen this in tech before and even publicly when Mark Zuckerberg has made these decisions before to invest heavily. It didn’t always pay off. I just want to point out, it didn’t always pay off. Yeah, it did not always pay off. Although you and I technically are in the metaverse right now, by some definition. [Laughs] Right. But I think that’s something, and there’s an interesting number in the S-1 that 80 percent of revenue in the last three months comes from models released in the last six months. So then you say, “Okay, 20 percent of the models are like Opus 4.5 in earlier versions.” One thing going forward is that if you’re a frontier model company, you always need to be at the frontier and it’s incredibly competitive. Wait, can I ask a really dumb question about that? Yeah. Why? I think the heart of my curiosity about the industry right now is if you enabled some bleeding-edge technology that could revolutionize the entire world, at some point, the most profitable thing to do is to just go play it out in all the different verticals, right? It’s not to go make the next one. It’s actually to run an efficient model in legal services and medicine and wherever else that there hasn’t been diffusion of AI yet. This idea that you always have to be at the frontier, that Anthropic always has to be competing with Google and OpenAI and whoever else, I get it from their self-conception. But from a business point of view, an AI-enabled business is going to throw out more money and spend more money with me, the AI provider, and that isn’t necessarily related to being at the frontier. There are a few portions of that. For new verticals, and this is very cyber specific, if an adversary is using a frontier model, you need to be defending with a frontier model. Fair enough. When we talk to some enterprises, it’s not like an email summary where I can run that on open source or Sonnet. There are just certain verticals where having... [For example,] if you were in a legal case as a defendant, would you be okay if your lawyer was using a non-frontier model if the prosecution— [Laughs] I got bad news for you about what’s going on in the legal market right now. The competitive dynamics do dictate that. I think from a go-forward perspective, we’ve seen this with open source too catching up in one point, but the demand will be there. [SemiAnalysis CEO] Dylan [Patel] says this a lot. The demand will always be there for frontier intelligence, especially in competitive industries. And there are certain tasks, as you go towards more labor replacement versus labor augmentation, where that also is the case. At the same time, they are getting more vertical. If you go look at job postings or what they’re hiring for, they’re putting out more of these SKUs and areas, and there’s a lot of beta testing going on like Claude for financial services, Claude for legal, their cyber program. They’re giving away 25,000 of credits per month for people in their cyber program. That’ll be a huge SKU for them in 2027. Those verticalized areas and then ones that are specifically where you need to be... It’s more adversarial, I should say, or competitive, are the main reasons why. But we can both agree there are areas like email summary and work that definitely doesn’t need to happen [at the frontier]. I’ll just make a dumb comparison to the iPhone. It’s iPhone season. I just reviewed the iPhone Duo. Apple kept the iPhone looking the same for several years now. They build all of the tooling for the new iPhone and then they just reuse it for two or three or four models to get all the value out of that investment back before they move on to the next thing. Apple puts out a new iPhone, and it keeps selling the old iPhone for a while to get more value out of that investment and that development program. The AI industry does not seem to be doing that. All of their emphasis is on developing the next new thing, deprecating the old thing pretty fast, and moving you onto the new expensive product, while at the same time they’re building the next new expensive product. At some point it feels like that will rationalize, that there will be something that is worth just collecting margin from while they go invest in the new thing. I just can’t figure out where Anthropic sits in that cycle. I mean, we do see this. Open source token volumes are picking up and there’s a lot of areas, yes, where the open source models have become good enough. I think on a go-forward basis, you’re like, “Okay, was that because of distillation?” And then the frontier labs have some defensibility actually going forward. I think when we talk to clients, it’s also about how we actually think about frontier versus open source. So something like a Sonnet type model, if you want to do the iPhone 18 versus the SE type analogy. We do see that dynamic, and obviously with open source, it’s a question of how much that can take. Two, because we’re so early in these verticals, we don’t know what’s going to be fully agentic. There’s no human in the loop where the harness actually has, I should say, some value and defensibility to it. The big area I’d look at here, especially when we talk to enterprises today, is only the coders are allowed to use the frontier models at a lot of these enterprises. If you’re a non-coder, some of these companies just limit you to Sonnet, if you’re an Anthropic customer. That’s reflective of how management views and wants to budget for this, what frontier intelligence is actually worth to them in certain areas. In my financial analyst brain, Claude could not build a good financial model six months ago. It’s getting better if you connect it to the right areas, but we’ve gone from something like, “I needed a junior analyst six months ago,” to, “Maybe I don’t as much anymore,” and then, “Will I have a full junior analyst at my disposal anytime or multiple pretty quickly, if I have unlimited token budget?” We just look at that across every vertical and major job category. The time horizon in each of those categories is going to be different. That’s just one of the bigger questions I have: How quickly do they get to where they think they can go? I want to dig in on some of the numbers here. The one that jumped out in all of the comment sections on all of the forums and all of our articles yesterday was $80 billion. Anthropic lost $80 billion [in the first half of 2026]. That is related to a technical charge. Can you just explain the $80 billion? Because it doesn’t seem particularly relevant to the revenue and profits they’re talking about. Yeah, it’s a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much and they’ve issued warrants or convertible notes. You have to account for that in your balance sheet. It’s just a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much since they issued these warrants and notes. That’s something you would always back out. You can argue on stuff like stock-based compensation. Should we really be thinking about that on a non-GAAP cash basis? Because it’s non-cash, if I just hand employees shares, I have to account for that on my income statement, but I’m not actually handing them pure cash out of my bank balance. So it’s not an area like that. It gets the accounting, the high level. If you don’t know accounting, it looks bad, but it’s because they’ve grown so much and their valuation has gone up so much. Some of the argument here about that charge is that Amazon was the other party there. Obviously Amazon’s very happy because Anthropic is buying a ton of AWS and sure they’re happy the valuation has gone up, but over time Amazon’s going to get diluted this way. That’s part of the dynamic there. Anthropic is going to obviously IPO. They’re going to put a bunch of shares in the market. It’s very clear that over time they will issue more shares to raise more money. It doesn’t seem like they’re going to stop wanting to raise money anytime soon. How are you thinking about that in terms of just investment into a company like Anthropic, that your valuation might be going up, but your actual ownership stake might be getting diluted over time? The deals have always been very creatively structured. The number is they’ve actually only burned $10 billion of cash. They have $120 billion-plus of cash and marketable securities in the balance sheet today, and post-IPO, probably another $100 billion. It’s a great deal for both parties. They only really rent compute. It’s not like they have these massive capital outlays or even rent-to-own. You can make some arguments about certain accounting and there are these massive compute commitment obligations and that’s technically future debt, or that is sitting somewhat off balance sheet essentially. But from a dilution perspective, all tech companies dilute. Are they going to need to raise another $100 billion of debt or equity at some point? Possibly. Can they continue to creatively structure and finance future compute buildouts? Probably as well. I know there’s been a lot of angst about the future of compute financing and data center financing in the last few weeks. But if you’re Anthropic, if you’re a major lab, a hyperscaler or Broadcom or Nvidia that are backstopping a lot of these deals, that’s probably not going to change anytime soon. So I’m not particularly worried. As an equity investor, would I be worried about getting super diluted? I don’t think so. If you believe in this long-term AGI bull case and that Anthropic is going to be a leader in this, that probably shouldn’t worry you. You’re probably looking at a $10 trillion-plus business. They can outrun dilution at that point. Let’s talk about the compute commitments. I saw at least one analysis saying over the next 10 years, it’s $800 billion-plus in commitments to the various hyperscalers and neoclouds. That’s a lot. You’re saying that they don’t have that much money. They haven’t even spent that much money yet. Do you see them generating the revenues to pay off those commitments? Yeah. I think when people look at the headline commitments, the $500 to $600 billion number over 7 to 10 years, let’s call it, what they’re paying for compute today actually isn’t that many gigawatts. If you think about their spending right now, on average they’re close to $11 million per megawatt in spend, or $11 billion per gigawatt. If you take that back to the annual level and say, “Okay, the $520 billion number is over 70 years, for example, that’s really not that many gigawatts and they’re going to be well beyond…” When they get to something like 20 gigawatts, the future compute commitments that they’re running essentially is going to be well into the trillions. So yes, they are going to have the revenue to do so. It’s more about how much revenue they are going to have relative to how much compute. Two, the compute efficiency equation. If they keep getting a lot more revenue out of every inference megawatt, how much do you really want to invest in training and take margins to zero from a rental perspective? Because you can get to something where even 80 percent to 85 percent of their fleet is just on training and research at these kinds of margins. The revenue is going to scale pretty well. They’re not in any dire situations there. Unless we realize all this revenue disappears or people churn. It’s not like they have to hit a trillion dollars of revenue extremely, extremely quickly to achieve all this and pay for this. Unless you’re trying to build digital God and unless it doesn’t diffuse across the economy as fast as everyone wants it to. Those are bets, right? They’re huge bets. The numbers you look at, if you’re really bullish on this ramp into the digital economy, is Anthropic saying within their Fortune 500 customers, they have 50 percent of the Fortune 500 and that is just 0.1 percent of their total customers’ operating expenses. When you look at that on a per user basis, it’s like $8 a month if you believe OpEx doesn’t include the cost of goods sold. If you believe they include the cost of goods sold, it’s sub-$50 per month. They said the same thing. Of the top 5 percent of Claude Code users, they’re spending $18,000 a year on average, the top 5 percent of users. Their non-Claude Code users spend under $75 a month, well under $75. There’s this huge opportunity, especially when we talk to enterprises and these traditional buyers of IT software. Penetration is extremely low in traditional white collar work. That’s the big point, too, that there is a large ramp period here of both seats adoption and usage. You can make arguments of who’s going to win in this, but it’s obvious the frontier labs are going to get some portion of this and it’s going to be pretty material to net new ARR next year. One of the things that’s really interesting about that is we talk about the frontier labs, we talk about the hyperscalers — Anthropic has a lot of wild risk factors in this S-1, including that Claude might be conscious and kill us all. But one of the most direct and maybe easiest to understand is that AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud are both suppliers and competitors in some real way, particularly Google. And they say, “These relationships could turn.” They have a big relationship with SpaceXAI. Elon Musk is going to train Grok. They’re going to compete with SpaceXAI at some point. That relationship might become precarious. As you say, they’re only renting their compute. At some point, the market might force them to own more of their compute because their own competitors don’t want to lease their capacity to the leading company. How do you see that playing out? We definitely see both OpenAI and Anthropic going more direct and not owning the compute, but more rent-to-own, or going through an SPV as some financial sponsors do and producing the compute more directly versus renting. There are two points to this. Google, from one perspective, is also selling its external chips to customers and saying, “We don’t care to monetize this within Google Cloud or even allocate the share... If you think we’re very chip-constrained, we don’t even care that these are going to DeepMind or internal GCP compute for us to monetize. We’re just willing to become a chip seller.” Anthropic loves TPUs and there are 3.5 to 4 gigawatts-plus, and probably more in the pipeline, in terms of orders there of Anthropic buying these chips directly to then rent. So yes, the market is good. Wait, it’s not buying them directly to rent. So they’re buying them into a neocloud? Yeah, they buy them through an SPV, or the SPV buys them and then they rent it from the SPV. Got it. Okay. Even within Google Cloud or AWS or Foundry, Anthropic is massive — 48 percent of their business comes through the Bedrock Foundry and Vertex where people are paying through their existing cloud relationship to access these models. They’re not even talking to Anthropic. You don’t have to interact with the Anthropic sales force. You mentioned this earlier. This marketing channel where Anthropic gets a rev share. Right. If you’re AWS and you’re saying, “I’m running Anthropic compute for, let’s say, $10 million per megawatt, but now I’m getting 16 percent of $65 billion-a-megawatt plus the compute costs as well,” so we’re seeing margins at all the clouds go up right now. Part of it is CPU utilization is going up because of all the coding and then some on the [reinforcement learning] side, but these token-as-a-service businesses as we call them — so AWS Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Google Gemini Agent Enterprise platform, which is formerly Vertex — are actually massively increasing the margins on AI at these clouds. They’re benefiting as well when shareholders are giving them credit for this recently. In Q2, both Azure and AWS had extremely, extremely strong quarters, AWS specifically, on the back of Anthropic’s growth on Bedrock. Do you think that will keep Amazon from ever wanting to train its own frontier models? They’re doing a good job of letting AWS be the infrastructure for everybody else, but they’re one of the only big tech companies that hasn’t felt the insecurity of not having their own models. Yeah, it’s interesting. Amazon is very happy to serve a wide variety of customers and they have very little [frontier capability]. When we look at our estimates of training compute, they have the least of any hyperscaler, except maybe Oracle. It doesn’t seem like there’s much strategy there. I know Microsoft in the last two quarters has been talking about it a little more. AWS on the call has been talking about it a little more, but it’s not huge. They’re not doing it to the same extent that Meta is or trying to be competitive here or even Google with Gemini. Especially someone like Dylan will tell you, if you’re not trying to compete at the frontier, there’s really not a place for you, especially if you’re only dedicating a few hundred megawatts internally. One, internal use case is like serving Amazon retail, but then two, training. There are a lot of commitments to make to be good at this. It’s a conversation for a different day, but I look at these Microsoft job cuts and I see it as the glimmer of evidence that they’re going to try to compete in the future. They obviously got burned pretty badly by OpenAI. Yeah. They have, in the new agreement that they signed, the right to monetize OpenAI models for essentially not paying OpenAI anything within that agreement. They’re going to have some interesting things ahead where they monetize the OpenAI models or even through Microsoft 365 Cowork and Copilot applications where they’re not paying OpenAI anything for a frontier model. The other dynamic here, and you brought it up earlier, is over the last few weeks, there’s just been a lot of stress about neoclouds — whether they will succeed, whether they will fail. I think Elon Musk said there will be a guppy-like extinction event, which is just a brutal metaphor to use to describe a bunch of data centers. But this is a bunch of circular financing and Nvidia stood a bunch of them up and maybe the hyperscalers are just going to run away with it. Maybe Anthropic’s demand, because maybe they will want to own more of their own compute because renting it is precarious in all these ways. What do you make of the neoclouds? Do you think they’re going to survive the market actually shaking itself out as these companies go public? Elon obviously has some incentive to say neoclouds are going to be extinct. ClusterMAX said something else and just does amazing ratings of the neoclouds. There are a lot of neoclouds that are ex-crypto miners that are not good businesses and are not good at operating clusters. I just want to point out CoreWeave is an ex-crypto mining company, right? Yeah. I don’t mean CoreWeave, but there are others further down the list. CoreWeave, Nebius, and anyone that has backing or backstops from one of the major labs, hyperscalers, Nvidia, or Broadcom is going to be okay. It’s that longer tail. Hyperscalers have been 65 percent of CapEx and net new compute brought online. There’s 35 percent of the market that doesn’t have the balance sheets that the hyperscalers have. Both Google and Meta have recently raised or announced they’re going to raise. When we look at the big four hyperscalers, they don’t actually need to raise that money over the next two years, even though CapEx is growing from $1.2 to $2 trillion pretty quickly. But for a lot of these other neoclouds, if you don’t have that sort of backing, I think it is very hard, even right now, and becoming extremely difficult if you don’t have the backing or backstops from those players to keep building compute. It’s a very, very tough financing market. One of the things I think is really interesting about Elon in particular talking about neoclouds dying and obviously hyping up his own data center business is he’s trying to put them in space and to get away from the backlash in the United States around data centers in particular. We have a lot of coverage about data center backlash in the United States, it is slowing down a lot of projects. But at the rate we’re going, if you think the neoclouds are shaky, you might actually end up abandoning a bunch of GPUs and half-built data centers or have them tied up in financing agreements where they can’t be lit up. What do you make of that? Do you think we actually just need to go to space? Or do you think the market is going to rationalize and actually take advantage of all the compute that is currently allocated but not being used? We’ll rationalize more so. The market is very good at finding places to put chips here on the ground. Politically, we’ll see what happens next week with midterms and the fallout from that. Obviously, there are some very large sites that still have massive permitting problems. There’s the entire power equation as we look towards next year. The data centers will be built. There will be a method to get these built. The biggest thing — and the hyperscale CFOs have said this — from an overbuilt perspective and on a relative basis, it’s pretty cheap to build the data center shell. What they can do if they overbuild is they’re going to say, “We’re just not going to take delivery of the chip. We’re not going to buy chips. We’re not going to fill them up.” They’ll just sit empty and chipless. But the majority of the spend is on the chip side. So if we do end up in a place where we’re actually oversupplied from a data center perspective, I know that’s a little bit different. It’s the exact opposite of what the question was. They have said that from an ROI perspective. This comes back to that larger question of whether we are still going to be super supply constrained. A lot of people now, especially in the last three weeks, are talking about, “Are we in this massive glut of compute as we look towards 2028 actually?” Because the same thing we talked about from Anthropic going from negative 94 percent margins to positive 85 percent and compute efficiencies mean as you bring on more inference megawatts that are making a lot more revenue per megawatt, all else SQL, you need less compute. So it’s a question of whether we we going to have enough revenue in 2028 to justify the ROI on $2 trillion plus of CapEx. This is why I spent so much time asking about capability overhang and how good the models are today, because you can see some competitor that is less idealistic about AGI saying, “Actually, we’re going to do a bunch of forward-deployed engineers in all of these verticals where they haven’t taken advantage of AI and sell them high-margin inference because we’ll automate big chunks of their business and they’ll see the return.” Right now, a bunch of the Fortune 500 has not seen a return on AI spending. So if you’re actually just better at customer service and deployment and productizing the model, you might get way ahead of where Anthropic needs to be because they’re still thinking about AGI every single minute of every single day. I look at Dario standing next to Marc Benioff at Dreamforce and that dude does not want to be there right now. He wants to be thinking about the machine god. There’s something there where you can just see competitors coming up with an open source model and saying, “We’re actually going to productize this and we will actually take the revenue that everyone else is depending on.” Yeah, it’s extremely, extremely interesting. In the interim, that’s why it is getting more verticalized because you need something to bridge AGI where it just fully does the job, you need something to bridge the actual model today. [Laughs] Yeah. We’ll just take that for granted. To get there, you need some bridges of where it sits with the actual end user at some point. Everything is going to come down to this: Is there going to be some timing or adoption mismatch where we just don’t get the revenue at a certain point of time to justify that chase of “train and compute towards AGI”? That’s a risk. The other risk we look at is whether we get more models at the frontier even at the open source that are as competitive in coding, where token pricing across the frontier needs to be taken down, because like I mentioned earlier, there are lower switching costs. Even at SemiAnalysis, we went from 95 percent or 90 percent-plus of our usage at the end of Q2 was on Anthropic’s models down to 70 percent after the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT 5.6 and Astra. And then with Opus 5.5, it’s gone back to 90 percent-plus roughly. It does come back. Even the base of revenue today — and they’ve said that we have net revenue retention of 900 percent, so they’re seeing this massive, massive growth. This isn’t a traditional software business like ServiceNow or Workday, where you have just an incredible logo or gross retention of 95 percent to 98 percent and customers sign these nice three-year contracts, they never churn, they add some seats, and maybe they adopt another product that is being upsold. This is purely consumption. The other portion was the 20 percent drop in the last two weeks of the year versus the prior two weeks last year in token spend, because of the holiday season. You’re not going to do work code stuff, you’re not going to be coding for work during the holidays. This is extremely, extremely pure consumption business, even different from how we think about Snowflake or Datadog today in public markets. Obviously, Anthropic is not the only company that’s going to have an IPO. OpenAI is right next to them. They’ve delayed theirs. You mentioned earlier Anthropic is much more enterprise focused. I think OpenAI for a long time thought that Google wouldn’t react to them and they would just take the search business away and everything would be fine. Google obviously reacted for better or worse. Search is now AI Overviews. Looking at the Anthropic S-1, what are you looking ahead to with OpenAI? Because they are a more consumer facing company. OpenAI was 60-40 consumer, 60 percent consumer and 40 percent enterprise at the end of Q1. That didn’t flip for the first time until January or August to be enterprise focused. What they’ll tell you is enterprise business — because it was so consumer and subscription focused, this consumption business that’s 80 percent of Anthropic’s revenue — didn’t take off until a release of 5.6 and then with Astra. Those are really great models. OpenAI took the majority of actual net new ARR in Q3, but it’s going to take some time because what’s been in the Wall Street Journal, like negative 100 percent EBITA margins versus we’re seeing positive 11 percent here. There are some differences, some pretty big differences, in the business model where they just don’t monetize at the same rate that Anthropic does. That’s a little bit because the business makeup — the verticals, that consumer-versus-enterprise split — and that’s changing. What they’ll tell you is they see a really good Q4 and they have a much stronger enterprise sales function than Anthropic has. I expect them to come up, but I don’t think the financials are going to look as good as this even when they drop their S-1 maybe in early 2027. Do you think that’s why they delayed it? To get their financials looking better? Yeah, I think OpenAI had a really strong Q3. Enterprise grew 100 percent quarter-over-quarter versus the total business which was 77 percent. You get another strong quarter of enterprise here. If Opus 5.5 didn’t take a ton of share, that would put OpenAI in a much better position to tell the story. There are some other turns here between now and when Anthropic actually goes public. They’re going to do a roadshow. There’ll be some pricing events. What are you looking for from Anthropic? They did an investor day two or three weeks ago where they did give some more color. I think they’ll walk through why Q3 was so weak. Meta was a very, very large customer, probably over 10 percent. What’s been publicly reported is they went from 60,000 Claude Code seats down to 30,000. These token volumes didn’t disappear, they just shifted into Meta’s internal models. Anthropic started cracking down on anti-distillation, and that was 5 percent of revenue prior. I think they said 5 percent to 7 percent of revenue in the S-1 and stuff against their terms of service. So what’s here on the roadshows is a lot of this October acceleration after Opus 5.5. We believe that they’re back on track. If they were doing $10 billion of net new ARR per month in Q2 and that fell down to $4 billion in Q3, that they’re getting back on that $8 billion to $10 billion pace here in Q4. People want to hear about these new verticals, specifically cyber. They’re doing some patching until they have that full cyber SKU rolled out, but they’re definitely monetizing cyber today for vulnerability code scanning. These are not small contracts, I should say, with existing customers. I think they’ll start to message what the 2027 ARR growth path looks like. The other thing too is expectations management, keeping numbers low enough, not talking about AGI as much. [Laughs] It’s hard to do expectation management when your risk factors are like, “We could pose an existential risk to all of humanity.” [Laughs] Right. And so saying you do that — you’re going to achieve AGI at some point, you’re going to replace everyone’s jobs — but then trying to keep numbers low enough for Q4 and to have this massive beat the first quarter you become public and have a decent guide for 2027, it’ll be a nice mix of seesawing between that long-term vision and short-term expectations management. There’s a lot going on. Joey, this has been great. We’re going to have to have you back as these companies barrel towards actually being public and their economics become much more visible. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Thank you so much. I appreciate it. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! articles.title: The NYT Cooking app is testing AI recipe modifications
articles.summary: The New York Times is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it’s sparked some drama among users.
articles.body: The New York Times is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users. Last Friday, NYT Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.” One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe. Ko says it can also change the recipes around different pans and tools. Customized recipes are private and can’t be published or shared through the app. The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the NYT monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.” Some NYT readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience. When one user asked if there will be a way to disable the AI feature, Ko responded with, “No, not at this time,” and noted that the feature is “completely optional to use.” [Image: The tool adds a chatbot text box interface on the lower screen of recipes, and it requires you to agree to some terms and conditions before you use it. “Unbelievably disappointing to see,” said another NYT user. “I’ve always loved NYT Cooking and it pains me that the AI mandate has reached what used to be a wonderful and simple collection of recipes and notes from all sorts of different people.” This isn’t the first time that AI has been used by the NYT Cooking app. Ko says it was used to convert imperial volume measurements to metric weight measurements in recipes two years ago, and a feature was added last year that converts recipes to halve or double the original serving size. The comments on the new AI feature announcement post have since been closed, but NYT spokesperson Jordan Cohen tells The Verge that this is standard practice: “Comments on this article remained open for four days, with editors from Cooking taking care to answer questions, address concerns and engage directly with readers. We kept that conversation open to give readers a meaningful opportunity to share feedback and hear from the team. Closing comments on older articles is standard practice at The Times so that our moderators can focus on new discussions. We’re pleased to see that many members of our Cooking community are interested in exploring this tool and are already trying it out on our iOS app; they’re reporting good results.”

articles.title: US investigated Chinese spy plot aimed at Nvidia CEO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud company that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, sources have told the New York Times.
articles.body:
A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud firm that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, anonymous sources told the New York Times .

The executive, Alice Huang (or Huang Le), worked for Megaspeed and was photographed as one of multiple people hanging out with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during various business dinners in the Singapore region. U.S. intelligence agencies had been surveilling Alice Huang to learn more about her ties with China for about a year, the Times reports.

The concern, sources said, was that Alice Huang had grown so close to Jensen Huang that she could have been gathering information about Nvidia’s plans and the CEO’s efforts to convince the Trump administration to allow it to ship more advanced technology to China.

But an Nvidia spokesperson denied this, telling TechCrunch that the CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was the same as with any other regional customer.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The company also said, “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”

In 2025, the Times reported that the Commerce Department had investigated Megaspeed over concerns that it was helping Chinese companies sidestep AI chip export regulations by reselling restricted chips to them. Alice Huang was said to be a top executive for the firm at the time.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO Reveals The Risks Of Relying On Its Biggest AI Competitors
articles.summary: Anthropic's IPO filing details hundreds of billions in AI infrastructure commitments, exposing the financial risks of relying on cloud giants that also compe...
articles.body:
As the internet fills up with hot takes from the S-1 statement for AI leader Anthropic's IPO, let's talk about how this historic IPO highlights the massive stakes and enormous competition in cloud infrastructure—and how Anthropic's future will depend on its relationship with "frenemies" in AI infrastructure.

First, the big numbers. Anthropic has the potential to outbid SpaceX for the largest IPO of all time. SpaceX debuted in June with a valuation $1.8 trillion and has bounced around between a $1.75-$2 trillion, for months. It was the largest IPO in history both by capital raised and valuation achieved. Anthropic is looking to raise up to $100 billion with a valuation of $1.5-$2 trillion, rivaling SpaceX.

SpaceX is both a supplier and a competitor with Anthropic. Both build AI tools and infrastructure but also have a business deal together. They are frenemies. More on this later.

Anthropic's growth rate is astounding—its revenue grew 1,300% on a year/year basis to $16.3 billion in the 1H of 2026 . But its spending on compute and infrastructure is also growing like mad—a liability. The company has at least $542-$567 billion in compute spending commitments, mostly through convertible bond and equity deals with partners.

Anthropic's $807 Billion AI Infrastructure Challenge

The spending is one of the more intriguing elements of Anthropic's business. To continue its business, Anthropic needs an enormous amount of compute from some of the largest companies in the world. Many of these companies are also competitors, showing how complex and dynamic the AI infrastructure market has become.

Anthropic's approach to capital spending for compute has been creative. Realistically, it requires hundreds of billions in compute, but it doesn't spend all that with cash because it has managed to push a lot of that forward with convertible debt and equity deals with its frenemies.

With this approach, it only showed a net loss of $80 billion in the first half of 2026 and only showed a $500 million charge in capex. Most of its $80 billion in net losses was non-cash accounting charges, leading many Anthropic bulls to celebrate low losses and an imminet arrival of profits. It consumed limited cash on capex because a lot of compute was purchased with forward agreements.

Yet, the bulls seem to dismiss hundreds of billions in balance-sheet liabilities going forward. If it were you and I, we might consider it a large liability. As mentioned, in total, these convertible equity commitments (a liability that must be paid) add up to $800 billion. Anthropic will have to pay for this in the future with either a growth in earnings or stock, or a combination (most likely). The most likely scenario discussed is that the company issue more shares as its suppliers sell their equity positions, resulting in share dilution. This will be an overhang on the stock.

articles.title: You can generate and edit Google Docs files directly in Gemini chats now

articles.title: Ares CEO Says It’s Avoiding Backing AI Chips, Citing Complexity
articles.summary: Ares Management Corp. is avoiding financing deals to back the high-powered processing units that run sophisticated AI models, opting to invest in the data ce...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Ares Management Corp. is avoiding financing deals to back the high-powered processing units that run sophisticated AI models, opting to invest in the data centers that house them instead.

The asset manager has concerns that if it backs graphics processing units, it could get stuck holding assets that may be obsolete not long after they're released, said a person close to the firm, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.

"It's frankly a simpler underwriting with really attractive relative value," Chief Executive Officer Michael Arougheti said on a call with analysts Thursday, referring to financing data centers versus the computer chips known as GPUs.

"Without casting aspersions on GPU financing," Ares is finding more attractive investments in data centers and adjacent power infrastructure, he added.

The market for financing data centers is huge relative to the capital available to back them, according to Arougheti. The firm estimates AI capital expenditure needs to be around $5 trillion, with roughly $2 trillion needed for the build-out of physical AI buildings and adjacent infrastructure and $3 trillion for GPUs.

Arougheti's remarks come at a time of heightened investor anxiety around the AI sector, with both stocks and corporate bonds taking a beating in recent weeks on concerns that the massive spending on the sector may outstrip future revenues.

Almost every US bank and alternative asset manager has participated in the AI financing boom, on deals including Broadcom Inc.'s roughly $60 billion debt financing for chips that will be leased to Anthropic PBC and SpaceX's talks to raise about $40 billion for Nvidia Corp. chips. These chips cost multiples more than the data centers that house them, but typically depreciate over roughly five to six years.

Arougheti said on the firm's earnings call that he doesn't know "how to underwrite the decline and depreciation curves on that type of technology."

"At least for the time being, we're kind of sticking to the half of the market that we understand best and where our capability set is the deepest," he said

The bonds of CoreWeave Inc., the most well-known of the so-called neoclouds that lease GPUs to AI developers, plunged this month to levels that usually indicate distress. The cost to insure its debt has also spiked, reflecting concerns about the growing amount of borrowing underpinning the AI boom.

articles.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
articles.summary: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
articles.body:
Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said.

Thrive Holdings is the holding company spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner , as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says.

As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies.

Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said.

AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras . ADT already partners with Apple and Google and is expected to continue to do so. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards .

Note: This story was updated to include ADT’s current partnerships and to describe Thrive Holdings as a holding company.

articles.title: Rivian expands joint venture with VW to include AI assistant | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Rivian doesn't disclose if the value of its $5.8 billion joint venture will expand as a result.
articles.body:
The $5.8 billion joint venture between Rivian and Volkswagen Group is expanding to include AI assistants.

Rivian is now licensing elements of its AI voice assistant technology to Volkswagen Group as part of the broader joint venture, according to the company’s third-quarter investor presentation released Thursday.

Rivian didn’t disclose the licensing fees, payment terms, or which Volkswagen vehicles will use the technology. However, the AI assistant, which recently rolled out to Riv i an vehicles , could make its Volkswagen debut in the automaker’s low-cost EV called the ID EVERY1 . The small four-door hatchback is slated to be the first VW vehicle to use Rivian’s software and electrical architecture under the joint venture established in 2024.

The joint venture between Rivian and VW Group has already expanded once before, at least financially. The companies initially announced a joint venture valued up to $5 billion , but within months VW upped its commitment to invest up to $5.8 billion in Rivian by 2027. The initial tie-up, formalized through an independent company that kicked off in November 2024, focused on bringing Rivian’s electrical architecture and software to Volkswagen’s next generation of vehicles.

Rivian described the expansion to include elements of its AI assistant technology as “a proof point for the extensibility of the platform we’ve built in-house.”

Rivian spent two years developing its AI assistant before showing it off last year. That development work continued longer than expected, with the assistant finally rolling out in May 2026 to its flagship R1S SUV, R1T pickup truck, and in October to its new midsize R2 SUV.

Rivian has big aspirations for its AI assistant, which allows drivers and passengers to interact with the vehicle and control certain functions. Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe told TechCrunch onstage at Disrupt 2026 that the company has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. That capability could eventually allow Rivian vehicles to run AI agents created by other companies, including Anthropic.

The in-house AI assistant program also fits into Rivian’s push to become more vertically integrated — a strategy the company emphasized in its third-quarter earnings report.

“Our relentless focus on vertical integration remains a core competitive differentiator, allowing Rivian to seamlessly unify our hardware and software architecture to deliver significant value to our customers,” the company noted in its investor presentation.

That strategy led to Rivian overhauling its flagship R1T truck and R1S SUV , changing everything from the battery pack and suspension system to the electrical architecture, sensor stack, and software user interface. Its new electric architecture system and compute platform slashed the amount of wiring used and reduced the total number of electronic control units, or computers, used to control the vehicle from 17 different ECUs to seven. That foundation, Rivian argued, would allow it to build vehicles that can handle the computing demands required for advanced software and automated driving.

That technology caught the attention (and money) of VW, which has struggled to offer customers a modern software-centric vehicle found in competitors like Tesla.

Rivian made that vertical-integration case repeatedly in its investor presentation, noting that because it controls the entire technology stack, including compute, sensors, displays, lighting, and sound, “it can roll out rapid, vehicle-wide OTA updates that go well beyond the basics.”
